title: Knitted-on cast-on

content.text: The secret of the knitted-on cast-on is that every new stitch is made by working a knit stitch and transferring the resulting loop back to the left needle, so the cast-on edge and the fabric it feeds are formed from exactly the same action. This means a knitter who knows only the knit stitch can use it immediately, and the resulting edge stretches in proportion to the fabric above it rather than pulling tight as a thumb cast-on sometimes does.
You need a small ball of yarn and a pair of needles suitable for that yarn weight. A slip knot on the left needle gives you the first stitch to work into.

attrs.alt: Knitting on stitches (the modern knitted-on cast-on)
attrs.title: Fig. 345, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
Make a
slip knot
and place it on the left needle. This counts as your first stitch.
Insert the right needle into the slip knot from front to back, as if to
knit
Wrap the yarn around the right needle and draw a new loop through the stitch.
Transfer this new loop onto the left needle by inserting the left needle into the front of the loop from right to left, then sliding the right needle out.
You now have two stitches on the left needle. Repeat steps 2 to 4, always working into the last stitch made, until you have the required number of stitches.
Turn the work. The row of loops sitting on the left needle is your cast-on. Begin the first row of your pattern.
Where you'll see it
The knitted-on cast-on appears wherever a beginner pattern wants a clean, flexible edge without the setup complexity of a
long-tail cast-on
. It is also used mid-project to add stitches at the beginning of a row, for example when casting on extra stitches for a button-band extension or a thumb gusset worked flat.
Common faults

Twisted stitches on the first row. If you transfer the new loop onto the left needle with the leading leg at the back rather than the front, the stitch sits twisted. Check that the right leg of each new loop faces forward before you begin the first working row.
A loose, loopy cast-on edge. Working into the stitch too loosely leaves gaps. Snug the yarn gently after each transfer without pulling the loop off the needle.
Stitch count creep. Working twice into the same stitch (rather than always into the last stitch just added) adds extra stitches. Count after every five or ten stitches while you build the habit.
What to try next: once this cast-on is comfortable, try the
long-tail cast-on
, which sets up a firmer, more elastic edge in a single pass.

glossaryTerms.definition: A loop that tightens when the working yarn is pulled, used to anchor the yarn to the needle at the start of a cast-on.
The fundamental knitting action: the needle enters from front to back, yarn wraps around, a new loop is drawn through and the old stitch drops off.
A cast-on worked from a single length of yarn held over thumb and index finger, producing a firm, stretchy edge in one pass.

sourceNotes: Technique derived from Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 345. Public domain. Dillmont calls this 'knitting on stitches'. Method in wide use in Weldon's Practical Knitting series (1880s onward). Both sources are public domain.

title: Picot cast-on

content.text: The secret of the picot cast-on is that a small group of stitches is cast on, a
cast-off

closes the group into a tiny loop, and the process repeats so that each loop forms one decorative point along the edge. Because the points are locked closed by the cast-off action before the next group begins, they sit permanently and do not unravel if the edge is stressed.

You need yarn, needles, and the ability to work both a knitted-on cast-on and a basic cast-off. A crochet hook one or two sizes smaller than your knitting needles is a useful aid for returning stitches if you drop one.

attrs.title: Fig. 348, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
The following works a picot every 4 stitches. Adjust the grouping to vary the size and spacing of the points.
Make a slip knot and place it on the left needle.
Using the knitted-on cast-on, cast on 4 more stitches. You have 5 stitches total on the left needle.
Cast off 2 of those stitches: knit 2, then pass the first stitch over the second. One stitch remains on the right needle.
Transfer this remaining stitch back to the left needle. The small closed loop sitting below the needle is the first picot.
Cast on 4 more stitches using the knitted-on method. Cast off 2. Transfer the remaining stitch to the left needle. This makes the second picot.
Repeat step 5 until you have the required number of stitches, ending after a transfer step rather than mid-group.
Count the stitches on the needle (not the picot loops below) and begin the first row of your pattern.
Where you'll see it

The picot cast-on appears on the cast-on edge of baby garments, shawl borders, and lace scarves where a plain cast-on edge would be too severe. It is also used at cuff edges and along the lower hem of fine-weight garments to add a small decorative detail that survives washing.
Common faults

Picot loops pulling tight. The cast-off of 2 should be worked at the same tension as the rest of the cast-on. If you tighten automatically when casting off, the loops will be visibly smaller than they should be. Try working the cast-off stitches on a needle one size larger.

Stitch count off after each picot group. Because you cast on and then cast off within the same group, the count on the needle can feel confusing. Count only the stitches currently sitting on the needle; don't include the picot loops hanging below.
Uneven spacing between picots. This is usually caused by varying the number of stitches in each group. Keep a tally mark for each group as you work.
What to try next: the same picot principle applied to a cast-off edge gives a matching
picot cast-off
, which makes matching start and finish edges on shawls and lace collars.

glossaryTerms.definition: The action of closing live stitches so they cannot unravel, worked by passing one stitch over another along the needle. Called 'bind off' in US terminology.
A tiny closed loop formed at the edge of a knitted piece, made by casting on a small group of stitches and immediately casting off part of them.
A cast-off method that mirrors the picot cast-on, adding small decorative loops along the final edge of a piece.

sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 348, 'Casting on with picots'. Public domain. The method is also described in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s series). Public domain.

title: Knit through the back loop (k tbl)

content.text: The secret of knit through the back loop (abbreviated
k tbl

) is that entering the stitch from the back rather than the front rotates the stitch on the needle so the legs cross, producing a tighter, more upright column than a plain knit. The twist is not decorative accident; it is the direct physical consequence of changing the needle's entry angle.
You need yarn and needles. Cast on a small swatch of 10 to 15 stitches in any weight. The contrast between a plain knit column and a k tbl column is clearest in a smooth, plied yarn.

attrs.alt: Knit through the back loop (k tbl)
attrs.title: Fig. 351, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
Bring the right needle to the back of the work and insert it into the stitch from right to left through the back leg of the loop (the leg sitting behind the left needle).
The right needle tip will point away from you and slightly to the left. The entry feels more restricted than a standard knit stitch; that is correct.
Wrap the yarn around the right needle in the usual direction (anticlockwise from above).
Draw the new loop through the back of the stitch and slide the old stitch off the left needle.
The completed stitch sits twisted on the needle with its legs crossed. In the finished fabric this reads as a denser, more defined stitch than the one beside it.
Where you'll see it

k tbl is called for in twisted rib (knit stitches on right-side rows are k tbl to keep the columns crisp), in certain Eastern European and Middle Eastern stitch traditions where all knit stitches are worked through the back loop, and as a single-stitch correction after a
yarn over
that would otherwise leave a hole. It also appears in some
make-one increase
instructions where the lifted bar is worked through the back loop to close the increase neatly.
Common faults

Working the front leg instead of the back leg. If the stitch on the needle looks the same as a plain knit stitch in the finished fabric, check your entry point. The needle should enter at the back of the needle, not the front.
Dropped stitch when drawing the loop through. The restricted angle makes the draw-through slightly harder. Keep the stitch close to the tip of the left needle so there is less distance to travel.
Tighter overall fabric. k tbl consistently tightens
tension
by roughly half a stitch per 10 cm compared with plain knit. If a pattern calls for a full section of twisted stitches, re-swatch with a larger needle size.
What to try next: pair k tbl with
purl through the back loop
to work a full twisted rib.

glossaryTerms.definition: Abbreviation for 'knit through the back loop'. The needle enters the back leg of the stitch, twisting it as it is worked.
A deliberate wrap of the yarn over the needle between stitches, creating a new loop and, in lace, an intentional hole.
An increase worked by lifting the horizontal bar between two stitches onto the left needle and knitting into it, usually through the back loop to avoid a hole.
The number of stitches and rows per 10 cm in a given yarn on a given needle size. Called 'gauge' in US knitting.

sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 351. Public domain. Method also described in Mary Thomas, Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). Out of copyright in UK/EU.

title: Yarn over (yo)

content.text: The secret of the
yarn over

(abbreviated yo) is that it is nothing more than the yarn being wrapped once around the needle without entering any existing stitch, so it creates both a new stitch and, when worked on the return row, an eyelet hole. Every piece of lace knitting is built from this one action combined with a corresponding decrease.
You need yarn and needles. Practise on a flat swatch of at least 15 stitches in a smooth yarn so the eyelet holes read clearly.

attrs.title: Fig. 353, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
The wrap position depends on the stitches on either side. The three most common situations are covered below.
Between two knit stitches (the standard lace yarn over):
After working the knit stitch before the yo, the yarn is already at the back.
Bring the yarn forward between the needle tips, then take it back over the top of the right needle. The yarn has now made one complete wrap around the right needle.
Work the next knit stitch in the usual way. You now have an extra loop on the right needle.
On the following row, work the yo loop as a regular stitch (knit or purl as the pattern directs). This opens the eyelet hole below it.
Between a purl and a knit stitch:
After the purl stitch the yarn is already at the front. Take it over the top of the right needle and back to the back. This single movement is the yo.
Between a knit and a purl stitch (yarn forward):
After the knit stitch, bring the yarn forward between the needle tips, over the top of the right needle, and forward again between the tips. The yarn ends at the front ready for the next purl.
Where you'll see it
Yarn overs are the foundation of all
lace
knitting, appearing paired with a matching decrease to keep the stitch count constant. They also occur in
eyelet

buttonholes (a single yo with a k2tog removes one stitch and adds one back), in increase sequences where the hole is wanted, and in brioche knitting where the yo and slip stitch together form the brioche unit.
Common faults
Missed yarn over. The yarn is brought forward but not taken over the needle, so no new stitch is formed. Check that the yarn completes a full wrap over the needle tip before the next stitch.

Accidental double yo. Taking the yarn forward, over, forward again and over again before the next knit stitch wraps the needle twice. Unless the pattern calls for a double yo, this adds an unwanted stitch.
Eyelet closed on the return row. If the yo loop is worked
through the back loop
, it twists closed and the hole disappears. On the return row, insert the needle into the front leg of the yo as for a standard stitch.
What to try next: combine yarn overs with
k2tog
and
ssk
to begin working simple lace patterns.

glossaryTerms.definition: A wrap of the working yarn over the right needle between stitches, creating a new loop. Worked as a stitch on the following row, it leaves an eyelet hole below it.
Knitted fabric with a regular pattern of eyelet holes formed by yarn overs balanced with matching decreases.
A deliberate hole in knitted fabric, formed by a yarn over paired with a decrease on the same row.

sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 353. Public domain. Mary Thomas, Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). Out of copyright UK/EU. The between-purl-and-knit and between-knit-and-purl positions are described in Weldon's Practical Knitter series (1880s). Public domain.

title: Purl through the back loop (p tbl)

content.text: The secret of purl through the back loop (abbreviated
p tbl

) is that the needle must enter from the far side of the back leg and exit toward you, which is the reverse of a standard purl entry, crossing the stitch and twisting the resulting column in the same way that
k tbl
does on right-side rows.
You need yarn and needles. Work a small swatch alternating standard purl stitches with p tbl stitches on a wrong-side row to see the twist difference clearly when the swatch is turned.

attrs.alt: Purl through the back loop (p tbl)
attrs.title: Fig. 352, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
Bring the yarn to the front of the work as for a normal purl.

Insert the right needle into the back leg of the stitch from the right, going from behind the left needle and emerging to the left of the stitch. The needle tip points to the right and slightly away from you.
Wrap the yarn anticlockwise around the right needle (as for a standard purl).
Draw the new loop through toward the back of the work and slide the old stitch off the left needle.
On the right side, the corresponding column will appear as a twisted knit stitch.
Where you'll see it

p tbl is paired with k tbl on the wrong-side rows of twisted rib to keep the purl troughs tight and uniform. It also appears in travelling-stitch patterns where a column of stitches shifts diagonally, and in certain sock-heel constructions where a twisted-stitch fabric adds durability.
Common faults

Needle inserted into the front leg. The entry angle for p tbl is less intuitive than k tbl. If the stitch does not look twisted on the right side, the needle likely entered the front leg. The right-needle tip must pass behind the left needle before entering the stitch.
Yarn caught on left needle. When drawing the new loop through, the yarn can snag on the left needle. Keep the stitch near the tip of the left needle to reduce friction.

Tension noticeably tighter on wrong-side rows. Like k tbl, p tbl pulls the fabric tighter than its untwisted equivalent. If twisted rib is pulling on wrong-side rows, try the p tbl stitches on a needle one size larger, held in the right hand alone for those stitches.
What to try next: combine p tbl on wrong-side rows with k tbl on right-side rows to work twisted rib, which gives a crisper column definition than standard
rib

glossaryTerms.definition: Abbreviation for 'purl through the back loop'. The needle enters the back leg of the stitch from the far right, crossing the stitch and twisting the resulting column.
A fabric formed by alternating columns of knit and purl stitches, producing vertical ridges with built-in elasticity.
Rib worked with k tbl on knit stitches (and often p tbl on purl stitches) so every column is crossed, giving a denser, more defined texture than standard rib.

sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 352. Public domain. Mary Thomas, Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). Out of copyright UK/EU.

title: Heel turn

content.text: The secret of the heel turn is that a series of
short rows

builds a three-dimensional cup shape from a flat strip, and a decrease worked at the turning point joins the live stitches left on hold each time so no gap or hole remains in the heel cup. The geometry is surprising until you see it: rows of decreasing length, each anchored by one more stitch, naturally curve the fabric around a corner.

You need a set of double-pointed needles or a circular needle, yarn appropriate for socks (fingering or 4-ply weight works well), and a basic understanding of working in the round and of slip stitches. The heel flap leading into the turn is usually worked flat on half the sock's stitch count.

attrs.title: Fig. 357, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
The example below uses a heel flap of 32 stitches (half a 64-stitch sock). Adjust the numbers proportionally for other stitch counts.
Set-up row (right side): Knit 18 stitches, ssk, knit 1, turn. Leave the remaining 11 stitches unworked on the left needle.
Wrong-side row: Slip 1 purlwise with yarn in front, purl 5, p2tog, purl 1, turn. Leave the remaining stitches unworked.
Right-side row: Slip 1 purlwise with yarn in back, knit to 1 stitch before the gap,
ssk
(knitting the stitch on each side of the gap together), knit 1, turn.
Wrong-side row: Slip 1 purlwise with yarn in front, purl to 1 stitch before the gap, p2tog, purl 1, turn.
Repeat steps 3 and 4 until all the held stitches have been consumed, ending after a wrong-side row. The heel cup is now complete.

Pick up and knit stitches along both sides of the heel flap to rejoin the instep stitches and resume working in the round. The number of stitches picked up per side will be roughly equal to the number of rows in the heel flap divided by two.
Where you'll see it

The heel turn with flap is the most common heel construction in top-down sock knitting. It appears in the vast majority of traditional sock patterns from Weldon's Practical Knitter onward and produces a reinforced heel cup suited to hard-wearing use. The same short-row logic without the flap is used in the flap-free or short-row-only heel construction favoured in toe-up socks.
Common faults

Holes at the turn points. If the slip stitch at the beginning of each short row is not tight enough, a visible hole forms at each turning point. Slip the first stitch firmly and work the decrease (ssk or p2tog) tightly into the stitch on each side of the gap.

Wrong stitch count at the end of the turn. The turn is complete when all the held stitches have been consumed. If stitches remain unworked, an extra row or two is needed. Counting 1 stitch before the gap and 1 after the decrease on each row keeps the count predictable.

Ladder at the pick-up join. After the heel turn, a loose column often develops where the heel stitches meet the picked-up side stitches. Picking up one extra stitch at each corner and working it together with the adjacent instep stitch on the first decrease round closes this ladder.
What to try next: once the heel turn is comfortable, work the gusset decreases that follow it, which taper the foot back to the original stitch count over the next several rounds.

glossaryTerms.definition: Rows that do not travel the full width of the work, used to create three-dimensional shaping such as a heel cup, dart, or shoulder slope.
Slip, slip, knit: two stitches slipped individually as if to knit, then knitted together through their back loops. Produces a left-leaning decrease.
A small flat panel worked back and forth on half the sock's stitch count before the heel turn, adding reinforcement and structure to the back of the heel cup.

sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 357. Public domain. Heel-turn construction widely described in Weldon's Practical Knitter (Victorian series). Public domain.

title: Plaited stitch

content.text: The secret of plaited stitch is that every stitch is worked
through the back loop

on every row, so the legs of each stitch are permanently crossed and the resulting fabric looks braided or woven rather than looped. The crossed structure locks the stitches more firmly against each other, producing a denser, firmer cloth from the same yarn and needle size that would give an open stocking stitch.

You need yarn and needles. Compare a plaited swatch to a stocking stitch swatch of the same size: the plaited version will be noticeably narrower and feel stiffer before blocking. Allow for this by going up one needle size if you want to match a stocking-stitch
tension
swatch.

attrs.alt: Plaited stitch fabric showing the braided surface
attrs.title: Fig. 382, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
Cast on any number of stitches.
Right-side row: knit every stitch through the back loop (k tbl) across.
Wrong-side row: purl every stitch through the back loop (p tbl) across.
Repeat rows 2 and 3. The right side of the fabric will show a closely packed braided surface. The wrong side will look similar but with the braid direction slightly different.
Where you'll see it

Plaited stitch appears in Victorian knitting manuals as a sturdy fabric for stocking legs, children's garments, and domestic cloths. In Eastern European and Balkan knitting traditions it is the default stitch for garment fabric, not a textured variation. It also turns up in sock-heel reinforcement panels and as an all-over fabric in dishcloths where the added density improves scrubbing quality.
Common faults
Unintentionally tight fabric. The combination of k tbl and p tbl tightens
tension
more than k tbl alone. Swatch before committing to a full project: often one needle size up is needed.

Wrong-side rows slipping back to standard purl. The p tbl entry point is easy to lose track of. A stitch marker placed at the start of every wrong-side row as a reminder can help while the habit is forming.
What to try next: combine plaited stitch with a standard stocking stitch background to create textured stripe or panel effects within a garment body.

glossaryTerms.definition: The number of stitches and rows per 10 cm in a given yarn on a given needle size. Called 'gauge' in US knitting.
The most common knitting fabric: knit stitches on right-side rows, purl stitches on wrong-side rows, producing a smooth V-stitch face and a bumpy reverse. Called 'stockinette' in US terminology.
Knitted fabric in which every stitch is worked through the back loop on every row, crossing the stitch legs to produce a braided-looking, denser surface.

sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 382. Public domain. Also described in Mary Thomas, Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). Out of copyright UK/EU.

title: Knot stitch and bobble

content.text: The secret of both the knot stitch and the
bobble

is that multiple loops are created from a single stitch and then immediately closed back down to one loop, trapping the extra yarn inside a small mound that protrudes from the fabric surface. The distinction between the two is one of scale and method: a knot stitch closes the extra loops on the same row by passing the earlier stitches over the last one, while a bobble works several short rows before closing, making a larger and more pronounced bump.

You need yarn, needles, and the ability to work knit and purl stitches. Bobbles are easier to learn in an aran or chunky weight where the action is visible; the same principle applies to finer weights once the motion is familiar.

attrs.title: Fig. 354, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
Knot stitch (closes on the same row):
On a right-side row, work to the position of the knot.
Into the next stitch, work (knit 1, purl 1, knit 1) without dropping the original stitch from the left needle. You have 3 new stitches from the one stitch.
Drop the original stitch from the left needle. You now have 3 stitches on the right needle where there was 1.
Pass the second stitch on the right needle over the third. Then pass the first stitch over the third. One stitch remains: the knot.
Bobble (MB: make bobble, using 5 stitches from 1):
On a right-side row, work to the bobble position.
Into the next stitch work (k1, p1, k1, p1, k1) without dropping the original stitch. 5 stitches from 1.
Turn the work so the wrong side faces you. Purl across the 5 bobble stitches only.
Turn. Knit across the 5 bobble stitches.
Turn. Purl 2 together, purl 1, purl 2 together. 3 stitches remain.
Turn. Slip 1, knit 2 together, pass the slipped stitch over. 1 stitch remains. The bobble is closed. Resume working across the main row.
Where you'll see it

Knot stitches appear in traditional lace and textured stitch patterns as small surface details. Bobbles are a standard element of Aran patterning, where they punctuate cable panels and represent specific visual motifs (blackberries, clover) in the Aran design vocabulary.
Common faults

Flat bobble. Working only 3 stitches instead of 5, or skipping the short rows entirely, produces a flat nub rather than a proud bobble. The short rows are what push the extra yarn forward into a dome.

Bobble sits sideways. If the short rows are worked for 3 rows rather than 2 (i.e., two knit rows and one purl row), the extra length tips the bobble to one side. Keep to the row count: 1 purl, 1 knit, 1 decrease purl, 1 decrease knit.
Loose tails beside the bobble. The yarn at each turning point within the bobble can leave a small loop at the base. Work the first stitch of each bobble row firmly to prevent this.
What to try next: work a bobble within a cable panel to explore the Aran combination of texture and structure that makes that stitch family distinctive.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small three-dimensional knob worked from a single stitch by increasing into it, working short rows across the extra stitches, then decreasing back to one stitch.
A knitting tradition of cable and textured stitch combinations originating from the Aran Islands, typically worked in unspun or lightly spun wool.
A surface texture stitch in which multiple stitches are worked from one and immediately closed back to one on the same row, producing a small knotted nub.

sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 354. Public domain. Bobble construction also drawn from Weldon's Practical Knitter series (1880s). Public domain.

title: One-colour brioche

content.text: The secret of one-colour
brioche

is that every stitch is either a brioche knit (working a slipped stitch together with the yarn over that was placed in front of it on the previous row) or a brp (the same principle on the purl side), so every stitch is worked over two rows rather than one, producing the tall, squishy columns that characterise the fabric.

You need yarn and needles. Work in a smooth dk or aran weight yarn to learn the rhythm before tackling finer weights. The fabric grows half as quickly as stocking stitch because each stitch takes two passes.
Step by step

Abbreviations used: brk = brioche knit; brp = brioche purl; sl1yo = slip 1 stitch purlwise with yarn held in front, then take yarn over the needle to the back (creating both the slip and the yarn over).
Cast on an odd number of stitches. Row 1 (set-up, worked once only): *k1, sl1yo; repeat from * to last stitch, k1.
Row 2 (brioche row A): *brk1 (knit the slipped stitch together with its yarn over), sl1yo; repeat from * to last stitch, brk1.
Row 3 (brioche row B): *sl1yo, brp1 (purl the slipped stitch together with its yarn over); repeat from * to last stitch, sl1yo. End k1 if working flat with a selvedge stitch.
Repeat rows 2 and 3 for the fabric. The two-row repeat is the complete brioche cycle.
To cast off, work a standard cast-off but note that each brk stitch counts as 1 stitch, not 2, so the stitch count on the needle feels halved compared with a standard fabric.
Where you'll see it

One-colour brioche produces the classic reversible rib-like fabric used for cowls, scarves, and hat brims where the same face reads from both sides. It is also the foundation stitch for two-colour brioche, which adds a second yarn colour to each of the two brioche rows.
Common faults

Accidental increases from double yarn overs. The sl1yo must be one slip plus one yarn over, not two yarn overs. Check that the yarn is taken forward before slipping the stitch and then taken over the needle, not wrapped a second time.

Stitch count halving or doubling unexpectedly. Brioche stitches on the needle look like two loops sitting together; counting them as two rather than one inflates the count. Count only the brk stitches (the paired loop) as one stitch each.
Missed yarn over produces a hole and a decrease. If the yarn over is skipped on the sl1yo, the following brk works the slip alone, leaving a hole, and the stitch count drops by 1. Place a
lifeline
every 20 rows while learning.
What to try next: once the brioche rhythm is established, move on to
two-colour brioche
, which uses the same brk and brp actions with alternating yarn colours to create the distinctive shadow-rib effect.

glossaryTerms.definition: A knitting technique in which each stitch is slipped with a yarn over on one row and worked together with that yarn over on the next, producing a tall, deeply-ribbed reversible fabric.
Slip 1 stitch purlwise with yarn in front, then bring the yarn over the needle to the back. Used in brioche knitting to set up the paired stitch for the following row.
A length of smooth yarn or thread threaded through all live stitches at a checkpoint row, allowing the knitter to rip back to that row safely if a mistake is found later.

sourceNotes: One-colour brioche stitch is a traditional technique found in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s) and widely described in Mary Thomas, Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). Out of copyright UK/EU. Modern brioche abbreviations (brk, brp, sl1yo) are now industry-standard per Craft Yarn Council conventions.

title: Two-colour brioche

content.text: The secret of two-colour brioche is that the two yarn colours are worked on alternating rows, never on the same row, so each colour occupies exactly half the brioche cycle and the stitches that appear to be one colour on the right side are the opposite colour on the reverse, producing a fully reversible fabric where the colours simply swap sides. Each colour is carried up the edge of the work rather than cut, so there are never more than two working yarns at once.
You need two balls of yarn in contrasting colours (referred to here as MC and CC), a pair of needles suited to the yarn weight, and a solid grounding in one-colour
brioche
. Cast on with MC.
Step by step
Abbreviations: brk1 = brioche knit; brp1 = brioche purl; sl1yo = slip 1 purlwise with yarn in front, then take yarn over needle.
Cast on an odd number of stitches with MC.
Set-up row with MC: *k1, sl1yo; repeat to last stitch, k1.
Join CC at the right edge. Row 1 (CC, right side): *sl1yo, brk1; repeat to last stitch, sl1yo. CC is now at the left edge; do not cut.
Row 2 (MC, right side): *brp1, sl1yo; repeat to last stitch, brp1. MC is now at the left edge. The two yarns alternate at each edge.
Row 3 (CC, wrong side): *sl1yo, brp1; repeat to last stitch, sl1yo.
Row 4 (MC, wrong side): *brk1, sl1yo; repeat to last stitch, brk1.
Repeat rows 1 to 4 for the fabric. Each four-row repeat is one full two-colour brioche cycle.
Where you'll see it

Two-colour brioche is used for scarves, cowls, and hat bodies where a reversible colourwork fabric is wanted. Because the two sides are mirror images in colour, no wrong side is visible when the scarf or cowl ends trail or fold outward. It has no direct ancestor in Victorian knitting manuals; the technique spread through the early 2000s knitting revival and is now widely taught.
Common faults
Working the wrong colour on the wrong row. Each colour must always work the same row in the 4-row cycle. Place a small safety pin of the corresponding colour on each yarn end as a reminder.
Yarn tangling at the edges. Because the yarns alternate at the edges, they will twist around each other after each pair of rows. Every two rows, swap the position of the two balls to undo the twist.

Dominant colour bleeding to the wrong side. In two-colour brioche, the MC should appear on one face and CC on the other. If both colours are visible on the same face, a yarn over was worked in the wrong colour, causing the brioche column to blend rather than separate.

What to try next: once the four-row cycle is automatic, experiment with shaping in brioche (brioche increases and decreases use brkyobrk and brLsl dec / brRsl dec) to work simple tapered cowl or hat shapes.

glossaryTerms.definition: A brioche fabric worked with two yarn colours on alternating rows, producing a fully reversible fabric where the colours appear on opposite faces.
Main colour: the primary yarn colour in a two-colour knitting project.
Contrast colour: the secondary yarn colour used alongside the main colour in a two-colour knitting project.

sourceNotes: Two-colour brioche is a technique that developed primarily in the late 20th and early 21st centuries. Description is original, derived from industry-standard brioche abbreviations per Craft Yarn Council. No direct PD source. sourceType: SYNTHESISED.

title: Intarsia colourwork: introduction

content.text: The secret of
intarsia

is that each colour block uses its own separate length of yarn, and that length is twisted once around the adjacent colour at every colour change so the blocks lock together at their boundaries without leaving holes. Unlike stranded
Fair Isle
colourwork, which carries all colours across every row, intarsia carries each colour only across the stitches it owns, keeping the fabric single-thickness regardless of how many colours appear.

You need two or more yarn colours, needles, and a supply of small bobbins or yarn butterflies (small hand-wound lengths). Intarsia is worked flat rather than in the round; knitting a motif in the round is possible but requires an adapted technique.
Step by step
Wind each colour into a small bobbin or butterfly of yarn. Long lengths tangle; 1 to 2 metres per colour section is practical for most motifs.
Work across the row in the background colour until you reach the first colour-change boundary.
Before picking up the new colour, wrap the old colour yarn anticlockwise once around the new colour yarn. This twist links the two sections. Drop the old colour; pick up the new.
Continue knitting in the new colour across its stitch block.
At each subsequent colour boundary, repeat the twist: the yarn currently in use wraps once around the incoming colour before being dropped.
On wrong-side rows, the twist direction reverses so the wraps sit on the wrong side of the fabric. On a wrong-side row, bring the old colour up and to the left over the new colour before dropping it.
At the end of the piece, weave in each yarn end separately along the colour boundary on the wrong side, rather than across the back of the neighbouring colour block.
Where you'll see it

Intarsia appears in any flat knitting with large distinct blocks of colour: geometric shapes, picture knitting (animals, letters, seasonal motifs), and the bold horizontal colour blocks found in 1960s and 70s knitwear. Because it keeps the fabric single-thickness it is preferred over stranded colourwork for large motif areas and for cotton or non-elastic fibres that do not forgive the uneven tension that stranding can introduce.
Common faults

Holes at colour boundaries. The most common problem: the two yarns were not twisted at the boundary. Check that the outgoing colour wrapped over the incoming colour before being dropped, on every row including wrong-side rows.

Tangled bobbins. Intarsia with more than 4 or 5 colour sections requires careful bobbin management. Work from left to right across the bobbins, untwisting after every second row by lifting the work and letting the bobbins dangle free.

Loose stitch at the first stitch after each colour join. The tension at a join is typically looser than in the middle of a colour block. Pulling the new colour slightly tighter on the first stitch after a join, then normalising on the second stitch, helps this.

What to try next: work a simple two-colour square motif (a small heart or diamond, 15 to 20 stitches wide) using an intarsia chart to practise the joins on a predictable shape before attempting larger or more complex motifs.

glossaryTerms.definition: A colourwork technique in which each colour block uses its own separate length of yarn, twisted at boundaries to prevent holes. The fabric remains single-thickness regardless of colour count.
A colourwork technique in which all colours are carried across every row, weaving in the non-working yarn at intervals at the back to form a double-thickness fabric with floats.
A small winding device or hand-wound yarn butterfly used in intarsia knitting to hold and manage each separate colour section without the yarn tangling.

sourceNotes: Intarsia technique is widely described in Mary Thomas, Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). Out of copyright UK/EU. Modern bobbin management and twist-direction guidance is standard craft practice; no single PD attribution. sourceType: SYNTHESISED.

title: Drop-stitch lace

content.text: The secret of drop-stitch lace is that a yarn over worked on one row is deliberately dropped off the needle on a later row, unravelling all the way down to the cast-on if no anchoring row sits in between, and the resulting elongated loop creates an open column of space that forms the lace pattern with no decrease needed to balance the stitch count. Because the dropped stitch is intentional and planned, the work does not go wrong; the open column is the finished product.

You need yarn and needles. A smooth yarn in dk or aran weight makes the drop columns easiest to see and control. The yarn should have some elasticity so the dropped columns bloom open rather than collapsing.

attrs.title: Fig. 387, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (Therese de Dillmont, 1886). Public domain.

content.text: Step by step
The following works a simple drop-stitch lace scarf pattern.
Cast on a multiple of 4 stitches, plus 2 for selvedge (e.g. 22 stitches).
Rows 1 to 3: knit across (garter stitch). These anchor rows prevent the drop from travelling past this point.
Row 4 (drop row): k2, *yo twice, k2; repeat from * across. The double
yarn over
creates two extra loops on the right needle for each stitch position, inflating the row temporarily.

Row 5 (elongated row): k2, *drop the first yo loop off the needle (let it fall), knit the second yo as a normal stitch, k2; repeat. The dropped yo unravels down to the anchor rows, creating an open column. The remaining yo loop closes the stitch count back to normal.
Repeat rows 1 to 5 for the desired length. The garter-stitch anchor rows and the drop rows alternate to produce the characteristic striped lace structure.
Where you'll see it

Drop-stitch lace is a common beginner lace technique because it requires only knit stitches and yarn overs with no paired decreases. It is widely used for scarves, shawls, and lightweight summer tops where open columns give a loose, drapey hand. It also appears as a decorative insert within an otherwise plain stocking-stitch fabric.
Common faults

Drop columns travelling too far. If anchor rows are not worked at regular intervals, a dropped stitch will unravel all the way to the cast-on edge. Count the anchor rows between each drop row and do not skip them.
Stitch count off after the drop row. Dropping both yarn overs rather than one leaves a hole and removes a stitch. Drop only the first yo of each double yo; the second becomes the working stitch.

Open columns closing up. If the yarn has no elasticity or is worked too tightly, the drop columns stay narrow rather than blooming. Block the finished piece by soaking and pinning the drop columns open while damp.
What to try next: once drop-stitch lace is comfortable, move on to traditional eyelet lace where a
yarn over
is paired with a decrease to form a stable eyelet hole rather than an unravelling column.

glossaryTerms.definition: A deliberate wrap of the working yarn over the needle between stitches, creating a new loop and, in lace, an eyelet hole.
In drop-stitch lace, the long open loop formed when a yarn over is intentionally slipped off the needle and allowed to unravel down to the nearest anchor row.
In drop-stitch lace, a plain row of knitting worked between drop rows to stop the dropped loops from unravelling further than intended.

sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 387. Public domain. The technique also appears in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s). Public domain.

title: SSK decrease

content.text: The secret of the
ssk

(slip, slip, knit) is that slipping each stitch individually as if to knit re-orients it on the needle before the two are worked together, so the decrease leans to the left and its leading leg reads cleanly on the fabric surface in the same way that a
k2tog
leans to the right. The two form a symmetrical pair in every lace and raglan construction that uses mirrored decreases.
You need yarn and needles. Practise on a swatch of at least 20 stitches in a smooth yarn so the lean of the decrease column is visible.
Step by step
Slip the first stitch from the left needle to the right needle as if to knit (insert the right needle from left to right into the front of the stitch and slide it across without working it).
Slip the second stitch from the left needle to the right needle in the same way, as if to knit.
Insert the left needle into the front legs of both slipped stitches, from left to right.
Knit both stitches together through their front legs in the normal way. Two stitches have been reduced to one, and the resulting stitch leans to the left.
Where you'll see it

SSK appears paired with k2tog in lace patterns (where the lean of the decrease directs the eye along the lace motif), in raglan sleeve shaping (left-leaning decreases on the right edge of the raglan seam, right-leaning on the left edge), and in the gusset decreases that follow a sock
heel turn
. Any symmetrical shaping in knitting relies on ssk and k2tog as its mirrored pair.
Common faults

Slipping as if to purl instead of as if to knit. Slipping purlwise does not re-orient the stitch, so the resulting decrease will be twisted rather than leaning cleanly to the left. The slip motion for ssk is always knitwise: right needle tip enters from left to right.

Decrease leaning to the right. If the finished decrease column leans right rather than left, the two slipped stitches were knitted together through the back legs rather than the front. After transferring both slipped stitches back to the left needle with the left needle, the right needle must enter from left to right through the front legs.
Loose stitch at the decrease. SSK can be slightly looser than k2tog because the re-orientation requires two separate slipping motions. Snug the working yarn gently after completing the stitch.
What to try next: practise ssk and
k2tog
on the same swatch side by side and compare the lean of the two columns before using them in a pattern.

glossaryTerms.definition: Slip, slip, knit: two stitches slipped individually knitwise, then knitted together through their front loops. Produces a left-leaning decrease.
A decrease in which the overlapping stitch travels to the left on the fabric surface, used to mirror a right-leaning decrease in symmetrical shaping.
A garment construction in which the sleeve and body are joined at an angled seam running from the underarm to the neck, requiring regular paired decreases along four lines.

sourceNotes: SSK is a standard technique described in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s series, public domain). The knitwise-slip method is the modern industry-standard form per Craft Yarn Council. sourceType: SYNTHESISED.

title: K2tog decrease

content.text: The secret of
k2tog

(knit two together) is that it is simply a knit stitch worked through two stitches at once, so the first stitch lies over the second and the column naturally leans to the right. It is the most direct of all knitting decreases: one action, no preparatory slipping, one stitch removed.
You need yarn and needles. A swatch of 20 or more stitches in a smooth, plied yarn shows the right-leaning column clearly.
Step by step
Insert the right needle into the next two stitches on the left needle at once, from left to right through the front legs of both stitches together.
Wrap the yarn around the right needle as for a standard knit stitch.
Draw the new loop through both stitches and slide both original stitches off the left needle together. Two stitches have become one, leaning to the right.
Where you'll see it
k2tog is the most frequently used decrease in knitting. It appears in hat crown shaping (where multiple k2tog rounds converge the stitches toward the top), in lace patterns paired with
yarn overs
to produce directional lace motifs, in raglan seam shaping, and in the
heel turn
as the right-side row decrease. Virtually every knitted object with any shaping uses k2tog at least once.
Common faults
Entering only one stitch. If the needle enters the first stitch only and then the yarn is wrapped, no decrease is made. Check that the needle tip passes through both stitches before wrapping.

Decrease column twisting. If the right needle enters through the back of both stitches rather than the front, the stitch will be twisted (a k2tog tbl rather than k2tog). Both front legs of both stitches should be in front of the left needle when the right needle enters.
Wrong lean compared to
ssk
. K2tog leans right; ssk leans left. If both decreases in a pattern appear to lean the same way, one of them is being worked incorrectly. Swatch both side by side to compare.
What to try next: use k2tog and ssk together in a simple lace pattern such as a yarn-over-and-decrease chevron to see how the lean of each decrease shapes the fabric direction.

glossaryTerms.definition: Knit two together: the right needle enters two stitches at once and knits them as one, producing a right-leaning decrease.
A decrease in which the overlapping stitch travels to the right on the fabric surface, used to mirror a left-leaning decrease in symmetrical shaping.
The sequence of decreases worked near the top of a knitted hat to converge the stitches to a small number, forming the rounded top of the hat.

sourceNotes: k2tog is a standard decrease described throughout Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s, public domain) and Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870, public domain). sourceType: PUBLIC_DOMAIN.
